chunks: 1- Musa ibn al-Qasim from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man vowed to walk to the House of Allah (Exalted and Mighty), and he became unable to walk. He said: Let him ride and offer a camel, for that will suffice for him if Allah knows effort from him.
2- From him from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr from Dharih al-Muharibi who said:
I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who swore to perform Hajj on foot, and he became unable to do so and could not manage it. He said: Let him ride and offer the sacrifice.
3- As for what Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Ali ibn Ri'ab from Abu Ubaydah al-Hadda' who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who vowed to walk to Mecca barefoot. He said: Indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) went out for Hajj and looked at a woman walking among the camels. He said: Who is this? They said: The sister of Uqbah ibn Amir, who vowed to walk to Mecca barefoot. The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: O Uqbah, go to your sister and tell her to ride, for Allah is富 from her walking and her bare feet. She rode.
4- From him from Ibn Abi Umayr from Rifa'ah ibn Musa al-Nakhas who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man vowed to walk to the House of Allah. He said: Let him walk. I said: But he becomes weary. He said: When he becomes weary, let him ride.

Do not see a contradiction between these two narrations and the first two regarding the obligation of expiation for the one who rides, because the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) did not say: Tell her to ride and there is no sin upon her. Rather, he ordered her to ride so that it would not be said that this is not permissible in any state. And if expiation is required alongside that due to the context of the camel, as explained in the first two narrations.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for someone who vows to walk to Mecca for Hajj but becomes too weak to continue?
ai.summary: These narrations from al-Istibsar elucidate the juristic principle of *rukhub* (riding) as a valid alternative to walking for Hajj vows when physical hardship arises, emphasizing that the Prophet’s instruction to the woman was permissive rather than obligatory. The text reconciles apparent contradictions by distinguishing between the permissibility of riding to avoid hardship and the continued obligation of expiation (*kaffarah*) if one chooses to ride instead of fulfilling the specific vow of walking. This reflects the Shia scholarly focus on balancing literal vow adherence with the Quranic mandate of avoiding undue burden (*la yukallifullahu nafsan illa wus'aha*).
